## 9. Wallet-vs-Account and Wallet-vs-Contract Distinctions

### 9.1 Wallet vs account on Solana

On Solana, wallets and accounts are fundamentally different:

- **Wallet:** a keypair with signing authority. Match reasons: "signer",
  "fee_payer", "sender", "receiver".
- **Account:** any pubkey (PDAs, token accounts, data accounts, vaults). Match
  reasons: "account_key", "writable_account", "readable_account".

The ingestion primitive is the same (`getSignaturesForAddress` or gRPC
`account_include`), but downstream interpretation differs.

### 9.2 Wallet vs contract on EVM

Both are 20-byte addresses, but:

- **Wallet (EOA):** controlled by a private key. Requires Transfer log scanning
  and native transaction scanning.
- **Contract:** has code at its address and emits logs. Uses `eth_getLogs` with
  address as log emitter.

Using `eth_getLogs` with a wallet address in the `address` filter returns nothing
useful because EOAs do not emit logs. This is the semantic error documented in
P0-W1 RFC Section 6.1 that V2 fixes.

## 12. Decisions Locked By This Spec

| # | Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Eight target kinds | wallet, contract, program, account, topic_filter, market, pool, protocol | Covers all target types from RFC Section 3.2 |

| 4 | Simple targets use `(kind, network, address)` uniqueness | Prevents duplicate ingestion | Deduplicates work while allowing different owners |
| 5 | Complex targets use `filter_spec_hash` for uniqueness | Deterministic hash of canonicalized JSONB | Prevents duplicate topic filters and protocol targets |
| 6 | `owner_id` is optional and control-plane-only | Not baked into raw data | Preserves RFC principle of target-agnostic Bronze |
| 7 | Addresses normalized before storage | Lowercase hex for EVM/HL, base58 as-is for Solana | Prevents duplicate targets due to case differences |
| 8 | `mode` controls connector invocation | backfill/stream/both with cross-connector coordination | Maps to the two-method Connector trait from RFC Section 4.2 |

   111→**Network row:** `solana-mainnet`, chain family `solana`, finality `probabilistic-slot`, block time 400ms.
   112→
   113→**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
   114→```json
   115→{
   116→  "target_id": "<uuid>",
   117→  "network": "solana-mainnet",
   118→  "source": "rpc",
   119→  "cursor": {
   120→    "last_signature": "5VERv8NMhzgC4...",
   121→    "last_slot": 298412345,
   122→    "commitment": "finalized"
   123→  }
   124→}
   125→```
   126→
   127→**gRPC checkpoint cursor:**
   128→```json
   129→{
   130→  "target_id": "<uuid>",
   131→  "network": "solana-mainnet",
   132→  "source": "grpc",
   133→  "cursor": {
   134→    "last_slot": 298412400,
   135→    "commitment": "confirmed"
   136→  }
   137→}
   138→```
   139→
   140→RPC and gRPC sources use different pagination primitives (signature vs slot) and
   141→have independent checkpoint rows keyed by `(target_id, network, source)`.
   142→
   143→### 3.2 Ethereum Mainnet
   144→
   145→**Network row:** `ethereum-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `probabilistic-block`, block time 12000ms.
   146→
   147→**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
   148→```json
   149→{
   150→  "target_id": "<uuid>",
   151→  "network": "ethereum-mainnet",
   152→  "source": "rpc",
   153→  "cursor": {
   154→    "last_block": 21500000,
   155→    "last_block_hash": "0x4e3a3754410177e6937ef1f84bba68ea139e8d1a..."
   156→  }
   157→}
   158→```
   159→
   160→Reorg detection uses `last_block_hash` comparison on checkpoint load.
   161→
   162→### 3.3 Base Mainnet
   163→
   164→**Network row:** `base-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `deterministic-block`, block time 2000ms.
   165→
   166→**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
   167→```json
   168→{
   169→  "target_id": "<uuid>",
   170→  "network": "base-mainnet",
   171→  "source": "rpc",
   172→  "cursor": {
   173→    "last_block": 25000000,
   174→    "last_block_hash": "0xabc123..."
   175→  }
   176→}
   177→```
   178→
   179→Uses the same EVM connector as Ethereum. `deterministic-block` finality means
   180→reorg detection is optional but `last_block_hash` is stored defensively.
   181→
   182→### 3.4 Arbitrum Mainnet
   183→
   184→**Network row:** `arbitrum-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `deterministic-block`, block time 250ms.
   185→
   186→**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
   187→```json
   188→{
   189→  "target_id": "<uuid>",
   190→  "network": "arbitrum-mainnet",
   191→  "source": "rpc",
   192→  "cursor": {
   193→    "last_block": 280000000,
   194→    "last_block_hash": "0xdef456..."
   195→  }
   196→}
   197→```
   198→
   199→Fast block times (~250ms) may require larger `block_chunk` sizes for efficient
   200→backfill. That is a connector configuration concern, not a network model concern.
   201→
   202→### 3.5 HyperCore Mainnet
   203→
   204→**Network row:** `hypercore-mainnet`, chain family `hyperliquid`, finality `instant`, block time NULL.
   205→
   206→**REST checkpoint cursor:**
   207→```json
   208→{
   209→  "target_id": "<uuid>",
   210→  "network": "hypercore-mainnet",
   211→  "source": "rest",
   212→  "cursor": {
   213→    "last_timestamp_ms": 1700000000001,
   214→    "last_fill_tid": 987654,
   215→    "data_types_covered": ["fills", "funding", "ledger_updates"]
   216→  }
   217→}
   218→```
   219→
   220→Timestamp ordering (millisecond precision) plus fill trade ID for sub-millisecond
   221→deduplication.
   222→
   223→### 3.6 HyperEVM Mainnet
   224→
   225→**Network row:** `hyperevm-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `deterministic-block`, block time 2000ms.
   226→
   227→**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
   228→```json
   229→{
   230→  "target_id": "<uuid>",
   231→  "network": "hyperevm-mainnet",
   232→  "source": "rpc",
   233→  "cursor": {
   234→    "last_block": 5000000,
   235→    "last_block_hash": "0x789abc..."
   236→  }
   237→}
   238→```
   239→
   240→HyperEVM is an EVM chain. It uses the standard EVM connector with a HyperEVM RPC
   241→URL. See Section 4 for the routing split.
   242→
   243→---
   244→
   245→## 4. HyperCore vs HyperEVM Routing Split
   246→
   247→HyperCore and HyperEVM are separate ingestion models despite being part of the
   248→same Hyperliquid ecosystem.
   249→
   250→| Property | HyperCore | HyperEVM |
   251→|---|---|---|
   252→| Chain family | `hyperliquid` | `evm` |
   253→| Network ID | `hypercore-mainnet` | `hyperevm-mainnet` |
   254→| Protocol model | Order book / clearinghouse | EVM smart contracts |
   255→| Ingestion method | REST API + WebSocket | `eth_getLogs` + `eth_getBlockByNumber` |
   256→| Finality | Instant (API-confirmed) | Deterministic block (sequencer-confirmed) |
   257→| Checkpoint model | Timestamp + trade ID cursor | Block number + block hash cursor |
   258→
   259→**Connector routing is determined by `chain_family`, not by ecosystem:**
   260→
   261→```
   262→Target on hypercore-mainnet → chain_family = hyperliquid → HyperliquidRestConnector / HyperliquidWsConnector
   263→Target on hyperevm-mainnet  → chain_family = evm         → EvmConnector
   264→```
   265→
   266→A Hyperliquid user wanting complete coverage creates targets on both networks.
   267→Cross-chain event correlation (e.g. bridging between HyperCore and HyperEVM) is
   268→a downstream Silver/Gold layer concern, not a Bronze ingestion concern.
   269→
   270→---
   271→
   272→## 5. Checkpoint Cursor Shapes (Summary)
   273→
   274→| Chain Family | Cursor Shape | Primary Resume Field | Reorg Detection |
   275→|---|---|---|---|
   276→| `solana` | `{ last_signature, last_slot, commitment }` | `last_signature` (RPC), `last_slot` (gRPC) | Not needed at confirmed+; slot-skip handling via gRPC `from_slot` |
   277→| `evm` | `{ last_block, last_block_hash, last_log_index }` | `last_block` | `last_block_hash` comparison on checkpoint load |
   278→| `hyperliquid` | `{ last_timestamp_ms, last_fill_tid, data_types_covered }` | `last_timestamp_ms` | Not needed (instant finality) |
   279→
   280→---
   281→
   282→## 6. Phase 1 Legacy Checkpoint Migration Guidance
   283→
   284→This section provides concrete guidance for migrating existing
   285→`indexer_checkpoints` rows to V2 `checkpoints` rows during the dual-write
   286→transition (P1-W4). It corrects three issues identified in local review.
   287→
   288→### 6.1 Current Legacy Schema
   289→
   290→From `migrations/20260217010000_add_indexer_checkpoints.sql`:
   291→
   292→```sql
   293→CREATE TABLE indexer_checkpoints (
   294→    chain chain_enum NOT NULL,             -- 'solana', 'hyperliquid', 'ethereum'
   295→    wallet_address TEXT NOT NULL,
   296→    last_signature TEXT,
   297→    last_slot BIGINT,
   298→    last_timestamp BIGINT,
   299→    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
   300→    PRIMARY KEY (chain, wallet_address)
   301→);
   302→```
   303→
   304→From `migrations/20260218000000_add_last_block_to_checkpoints.sql`:
   305→
   306→```sql
   307→ALTER TABLE indexer_checkpoints ADD COLUMN last_block BIGINT;
   308→```
   309→
   310→### 6.2 Solana: Persisted Resume Cursor Semantics
   311→
   312→**Important correction from earlier draft:** The Solana gRPC adapter
   313→(`adapters/src/solana_grpc.rs`) uses an in-memory `SlotCheckpoint` (an
   314→`AtomicU64` at lines 51-75) for `from_slot` reconnection. The adapter
   315→itself does not call `repo.save_checkpoint()` with slot-based state.
   316→
   317→However, the CLI ingest path (`cli/src/main.rs`, lines 147-155) calls
   318→`SolanaGrpcAdapter::fetch_history()` and then passes the resulting
   319→transactions through `build_checkpoint()` (`adapters/src/repo.rs`,
   320→lines 42-78) and `save_transactions_and_checkpoint()` (lines 607-621).
   321→This means **gRPC-derived Solana `indexer_checkpoints` rows CAN exist**
   322→in the database. These rows have the same schema as RPC-derived rows:
   323→
   324→- `last_signature`: set to the latest transaction hash (from
   325→  `build_checkpoint`, line 73)
   326→- `last_slot`: extracted from `raw_metadata["slot"]` (lines 54-59);
   327→  present on BOTH RPC and gRPC-derived Solana transactions because both
   328→  adapter outputs include `"slot"` in their `raw_metadata`
   329→- `last_timestamp`: set to the latest transaction timestamp (line 76)
   330→
   331→**The legacy `indexer_checkpoints` schema cannot distinguish RPC-derived
   332→from gRPC-derived rows.** Both sources produce identical checkpoint
   333→shapes through `build_checkpoint()`.
   334→
   335→**Resume cursor semantics by adapter:**
   336→
   337→| Adapter | Persisted field used for resume | How resume works |
   338→|---|---|---|
   339→| Solana RPC (`adapters/src/solana.rs`, lines 38-40) | `last_signature` | Passed as the `until` parameter to `getSignaturesForAddress`; the RPC returns transactions newer than this signature. |
   340→| Solana gRPC via CLI (`cli/src/main.rs`, lines 149-152) | `last_slot` | CLI reads `checkpoint.last_slot`, calls `adapter.checkpoint().update(slot as u64)` to seed the in-memory `SlotCheckpoint`, then `fetch_history` uses `self.checkpoint.get()` as `from_slot`. |
   341→
   342→**Why `last_signature` is the only authoritative persisted resume cursor:**
   343→
   344→- `last_signature` is the **only** persisted cursor that an adapter reads
   345→  directly for pagination. The Solana RPC adapter reads
   346→  `checkpoint.last_signature` (line 38-40) and passes it to the RPC as
   347→  the `until` parameter.
   348→- `last_slot` is used by the CLI gRPC path indirectly (CLI code seeds the
   349→  in-memory `SlotCheckpoint`), but it is **not** a V2 gRPC checkpoint
   350→  equivalent: it carries no `commitment`-level metadata, may not reflect
   351→  the gRPC adapter's actual in-memory slot state at process exit, and is
   352→  present on RPC-derived rows too.
   353→- Because RPC and gRPC-derived rows are indistinguishable in the legacy
   354→  schema, the migration defaults all legacy Solana rows to
   355→  `source = "rpc"` with `last_signature` as the primary cursor. This is
   356→  safe for RPC resume.
   357→- Legacy gRPC users will need to create fresh V2 gRPC checkpoints when
   358→  Phase 2 gRPC connectors start persisting `(last_slot, commitment)` state
   359→  directly to the `checkpoints` table.
   360→
   361→**Migration mapping for Solana:**
   362→
   363→| Old field | V2 cursor field | Notes |
   364→|---|---|---|
   365→| `last_signature` | `cursor.last_signature` | Authoritative RPC resume cursor; present on all legacy Solana rows regardless of original adapter |
   366→| `last_slot` | `cursor.last_slot` | Informational only; present on all legacy Solana rows; not promoted to V2 gRPC cursor state |
   367→| N/A | `source` | Default `"rpc"` for all legacy Solana rows; gRPC-derived rows cannot be reliably distinguished |
   368→| N/A | `cursor.commitment` | Not tracked in legacy schema; omit or default to `"finalized"` (RPC `getSignaturesForAddress` returns finalized by default) |
   369→
   370→### 6.3 HyperCore: Timestamp Precision Caveat
   371→
   372→**Caveat (corrected from earlier draft):** The current Hyperliquid adapter
   373→(`adapters/src/hyperliquid.rs`, lines 182-185) stores `last_timestamp` in
   374→the `indexer_checkpoints` table as **seconds** (epoch seconds). The
   375→conversion happens at line 200: `timestamp: (fill.time / 1000) as i64`,
   376→which truncates milliseconds.
   377→
   378→The V2 checkpoint cursor uses `last_timestamp_ms` (milliseconds). A naive
   379→migration that multiplies by 1000 (`last_timestamp * 1000`) would produce
   380→a value with **false millisecond precision**: the resulting timestamp would
   381→always end in `000`, which is not the actual sub-second time of the last
   382→event.
   383→
   384→**Impact on resume semantics:**
   385→
   386→- The current adapter resumes with `resume_ms = (checkpoint.last_timestamp * 1000) + 1` (line 184).
   387→- After migration, if `last_timestamp_ms = last_timestamp * 1000`, the
   388→  resume point becomes `last_timestamp_ms + 1`.
   389→- This is equivalent to the current behavior and does **not** cause data
   390→  loss.
   391→- However, events that occurred in the same second as the checkpoint but
   392→  after the truncated timestamp boundary will be **re-fetched** on resume.
   393→
   394→**Required replay/dedupe semantics for Phase 1:**
   395→
   396→1. The migration sets `cursor.last_timestamp_ms = last_timestamp * 1000`.
   397→   The value is understood to have second-precision granularity rounded
   398→   down to the millisecond boundary.
   399→2. On first resume after migration, the connector must be prepared to see
   400→   duplicate events from the final second of the previous run. The
   401→   existing deduplication on `(network, tx_hash)` in `raw_transactions`
   402→   handles this for transaction-level records.
   403→3. For fills specifically, `last_fill_tid` is **not available** in legacy
   404→   checkpoints. The migrated cursor omits `last_fill_tid`. The Phase 2
   405→   HyperCore connector should use timestamp-only deduplication until a
   406→   `last_fill_tid` is captured in the first post-migration checkpoint
   407→   write.
   408→4. New V2 checkpoint writes from the Phase 2 connector will store true
   409→   millisecond timestamps directly from the API response (`fill.time`,
   410→   `funding.time`, `update.time`), so the precision loss is a one-time
   411→   migration artifact.
   412→
   413→**Migration mapping for HyperCore:**
   414→
   415→| Old field | V2 cursor field | Notes |
   416→|---|---|---|
   417→| `last_timestamp` | `cursor.last_timestamp_ms` | Multiply by 1000; understood as second-precision |
   418→| N/A | `cursor.last_fill_tid` | Not available in legacy; omit |
   419→| N/A | `source` | Always `"rest"` for legacy HyperCore rows |
   420→| N/A | `cursor.data_types_covered` | Not tracked in legacy; omit or default to `["fills", "funding", "ledger_updates"]` |
   421→
   422→### 6.4 EVM: Network Reclassification Caveat
   423→
   424→**Caveat (carried from spec):** The current `Chain::Ethereum` variant
   425→(`core/src/models.rs`, lines 6-10) is used for all EVM-compatible chains.
   426→The repository maps it to the database string `"ethereum"`
   427→(`adapters/src/repo.rs`, lines 4-9).
   428→
   429→The migration defaults all legacy `chain = 'ethereum'` rows to
   430→`network = 'ethereum-mainnet'`. This is correct for deployments that only
   431→indexed Ethereum mainnet data via `Chain::Ethereum`.
   432→
   433→**If a deployment was indexing Base, Arbitrum, or other EVM chain data
   434→under `Chain::Ethereum`**, those rows will be incorrectly assigned to
   435→`ethereum-mainnet`. This requires manual reclassification.
   436→
   437→**Phase 1 must define the exact override mechanism before migration code
   438→ships.** Options under consideration (to be resolved in P1-W2):
   439→
   440→1. **Migration-time environment variable**: e.g.
   441→   `REDACTED` forces all legacy
   442→   Ethereum rows to a specific network. Simple but only works for
   443→   single-network deployments.
   444→2. **Migration-time configuration map**: a TOML or JSON map from
   445→   `(chain, wallet_address)` to `network` for targeted reclassification.
   446→3. **Post-migration reclassification CLI command**: a new CLI command to
   447→   reassign `network` on existing rows by wallet address or block range.
   448→
   449→The choice is deferred to P1-W2. This handoff documents the requirement
   450→so it is not lost.
   451→
   452→**Migration mapping for EVM:**
   453→
   454→| Old field | V2 cursor field | Notes |
   455→|---|---|---|
   456→| `last_block` | `cursor.last_block` | Direct mapping |
   457→| N/A | `cursor.last_block_hash` | Not tracked in legacy; omit (reorg detection starts fresh from V2) |
   458→| N/A | `source` | Always `"rpc"` for legacy EVM rows |
   459→| N/A | `network` | Default `"ethereum-mainnet"` unless overridden; see caveat above |
   460→
   461→### 6.5 Legacy-to-V2 Default Source Summary
   462→
   463→| Legacy `chain` value | V2 `chain_family` | V2 default `network` | V2 default `source` | Rationale |
   464→|---|---|---|---|---|
   465→| `solana` | `solana` | `solana-mainnet` | `rpc` | Legacy Solana checkpoints may come from either the RPC or gRPC CLI path but are indistinguishable in the legacy schema; `last_signature` is the authoritative persisted resume cursor (Section 6.2) |
   466→| `hyperliquid` | `hyperliquid` | `hypercore-mainnet` | `rest` | All persisted HyperCore checkpoints come from the REST adapter |
   467→| `ethereum` | `evm` | `ethereum-mainnet` | `rpc` | All persisted EVM checkpoints come from the RPC adapter; may need network reclassification (Section 6.4) |
   468→
   469→---
   470→
   471→## 7. Decisions Locked By This Handoff
   472→
   473→These decisions are frozen. Phase 1+ work packets should reference them, not
   474→reopen them.
   475→
   476→| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
   477→|---|---|---|
   478→| Three chain families | `solana`, `evm`, `hyperliquid` | Maps to three protocol-level ingestion models |
   479→| HyperEVM is `evm`, not a fourth family | `hyperevm-mainnet` in chain family `evm` | HyperEVM uses standard EVM JSON-RPC |
   480→| HyperCore is `hyperliquid` | `hypercore-mainnet` in chain family `hyperliquid` | HyperCore uses REST/WS, not EVM primitives |
   481→| Network IDs are `{chain}-{env}` lowercase | e.g. `solana-mainnet`, `hypercore-mainnet` | Stable, readable, collision-free |
   482→| Four finality models | `probabilistic-slot`, `probabilistic-block`, `deterministic-block`, `instant` | Distinguishes L1 reorg risk from L2 sequencer finality |
   483→| Checkpoint cursor is JSONB | Per-family cursor shapes in Section 5 | Different chains need different cursor fields |
   484→| `finality_model` is TEXT, not enum | Allows future refinement without migration | New chains may need new finality semantics |
   485→| RPC URLs excluded from `networks` table | Deployment-specific config belongs in spectraplex.toml or env vars | Network registry stores protocol facts |
   486→| HyperCore network ID is `hypercore-mainnet` | Not `hyperliquid-mainnet` | Avoids ambiguity with the broader ecosystem |
   487→| `block_time_ms` is nullable | HyperCore has no block concept | Prevents meaningless zero values |
   488→
   489→---
   490→
   491→## 8. Terminology Cross-Reference
   492→
   493→This section confirms alignment with the other Phase 0 specs.
   494→
   495→### 8.1 V2 Architecture RFC (P0-W1) Alignment
   496→
   497→**Taxonomy and finality alignment (verified):**
   498→
   499→- `chain_family_enum` values: `solana, evm, hyperliquid` — **matches**
   500→- Network ID examples: `solana-mainnet`, `ethereum-mainnet`, `base-mainnet` — **matches**
   501→- Finality model labels: four-value set adopted from P0-W3 — **matches** (RFC Section 3.3 updated)
   502→- HyperEVM routing: EVM connector with HyperEVM network — **matches**
   503→- `networks` table schema: `rpc_url` removed, `block_time_ms` added — **matches** (RFC Section 3.3 updated)
   504→
   505→**Checkpoint cursor shapes (partial alignment — P0-W3 extends the RFC):**
   506→
   507→- The RFC Section 3.4 documents baseline cursor shapes: Solana
   508→  `{ last_signature, last_slot }`, EVM `{ last_block, last_block_hash }`,
   509→  Hyperliquid `{ last_timestamp, last_fill_tid }`.
   510→- P0-W3 extends these with additional fields: `commitment` (Solana),
   511→  `last_log_index` (EVM), `data_types_covered` (Hyperliquid).
   512→- P0-W3 renames the Hyperliquid field `last_timestamp` to
   513→  `last_timestamp_ms` to reflect that the V2 cursor stores millisecond
   514→  precision directly (Section 6.3 documents the legacy second-precision
   515→  caveat).
   516→- The RFC's Section 3.4 inline JSONB comment (`{ last_signature,
   517→  last_slot, last_block, last_timestamp, ... }`) and the Hyperliquid
   518→  cursor field names have **not been updated** to reflect the P0-W3
   519→  refinements. This is a documentation gap in `design/V2_ARCHITECTURE_RFC.md`,
   520→  not a semantic conflict.
   521→- **The authoritative cursor field definitions for Phase 1 are in this
   522→  handoff (Section 5), not in the RFC.**
   523→
   524→### 8.2 Target Model Spec (P0-W2) Alignment
   525→
   526→- `index_targets.network` examples: `solana-mainnet`, `ethereum-mainnet`, `base-mainnet` — **matches**
   527→- `index_targets.chain_family` values: `solana, evm, hyperliquid` — **matches**
   528→- HyperEVM contract target routing: EVM chain family with `hyperevm-mainnet` — **matches**
   529→- HyperCore target examples use `hypercore-mainnet` — **matches** (corrected from `hyperliquid-mainnet` in P0-W3)
   530→
   531→---
   532→
   533→## 9. Open Questions For Follow-On Packets
   534→
   535→| Question | Deferred To |
   536→|---|---|
   537→| EVM legacy network reclassification override mechanism | P1-W2 |
   538→| Exact `block_chunk` tuning per network for EVM backfill | P2-W3 |
   539→| Reorg handling depth and reprocessing strategy for Ethereum mainnet | P2-W3 |
   540→| WebSocket reconnection and gap-fill protocol for HyperCore | P2-W5 |
   541→| Whether Solana gRPC checkpoint should also store `last_signature` for cross-source reconciliation | P2-W4 |
   542→| Additional EVM networks beyond the initial set (Optimism, Polygon, etc.) | Phase 1+ via data insert |
   543→| Commitment-level configuration per target | P2-W4 |
   544→| Cross-chain event correlation between HyperCore and HyperEVM | Phase 3+ |
   545→

# P0-W3 Network Model Handoff

Status: **Frozen**
Date: 2026-03-07
Phase: P0-W3
Branch: `codex/p0-w3-network-model-spec`
Depends on: V2 Architecture RFC (P0-W1) Section 3.3, Target Model Spec (P0-W2)

This document is the tracked, reviewable artifact for the P0-W3 network model
contract. It captures the locked decisions from the full network model spec
(`design/NETWORK_MODEL.md`, which lives in the gitignored `design/` directory)
so that reviewers can validate the Phase 1 contract on GitHub without accessing
local-only design docs.

No new scope is introduced here. Every item below is drawn directly from the
frozen `design/NETWORK_MODEL.md`.

---

## 1. Frozen Network Registry

Phase 1 migrations (P1-W2) seed the `networks` table with exactly these rows.
Additional networks can be added later via data inserts without a schema change.

### 1.1 Network Table Schema

```sql
CREATE TABLE networks (
    id              TEXT PRIMARY KEY,       -- e.g. "solana-mainnet"
    chain_family    chain_family_enum NOT NULL,
    display_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
    is_testnet      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    finality_model  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- see Section 2
    block_time_ms   INTEGER,               -- NULL for blockless chains
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
```

RPC URLs are excluded. They are deployment-specific and belong in
`spectraplex.toml` or environment variables, not in the network registry.

### 1.2 Chain Family Enum

```sql
CREATE TYPE chain_family_enum AS ENUM ('solana', 'evm', 'hyperliquid');
```

Three values. Maps to the three protocol-level ingestion models Spectraplex
supports.

### 1.3 Solana Family Networks

| Network ID | Chain Family | Display Name | Testnet | Finality Model | Block Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `solana-mainnet` | `solana` | Solana Mainnet | false | `probabilistic-slot` | 400ms |
| `solana-devnet` | `solana` | Solana Devnet | true | `probabilistic-slot` | 400ms |
| `solana-testnet` | `solana` | Solana Testnet | true | `probabilistic-slot` | 400ms |

### 1.4 EVM Family Networks

| Network ID | Chain Family | Display Name | Testnet | Finality Model | Block Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ethereum-mainnet` | `evm` | Ethereum Mainnet | false | `probabilistic-block` | 12000ms |
| `ethereum-sepolia` | `evm` | Ethereum Sepolia | true | `probabilistic-block` | 12000ms |
| `base-mainnet` | `evm` | Base Mainnet | false | `deterministic-block` | 2000ms |
| `base-sepolia` | `evm` | Base Sepolia | true | `deterministic-block` | 2000ms |
| `arbitrum-mainnet` | `evm` | Arbitrum One | false | `deterministic-block` | 250ms |
| `arbitrum-sepolia` | `evm` | Arbitrum Sepolia | true | `deterministic-block` | 250ms |
| `hyperevm-mainnet` | `evm` | HyperEVM Mainnet | false | `deterministic-block` | 2000ms |
| `hyperevm-testnet` | `evm` | HyperEVM Testnet | true | `deterministic-block` | 2000ms |

### 1.5 Hyperliquid Family Networks

| Network ID | Chain Family | Display Name | Testnet | Finality Model | Block Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hypercore-mainnet` | `hyperliquid` | HyperCore Mainnet | false | `instant` | N/A |
| `hypercore-testnet` | `hyperliquid` | HyperCore Testnet | true | `instant` | N/A |

### 1.6 Network ID Naming Convention

Pattern: `{chain_name}-{environment}`, all lowercase, ASCII alphanumeric and
hyphens only. Network IDs are stable and never change once assigned.

---

## 2. Four Finality Labels

The `finality_model` column is `TEXT`, not an enum, to allow future refinement
without a migration. Phase 1 uses exactly four values:

| Finality Model | Meaning | Applicable Chains |
|---|---|---|
| `probabilistic-slot` | Slot-based commitment levels (processed → confirmed → finalized). Slot skips possible. | Solana |
| `probabilistic-block` | Block-based with reorg risk. Finality via PoS gadget across multiple blocks. | Ethereum mainnet |
| `deterministic-block` | Sequencer-confirmed blocks. Final once posted to L1. Reorgs extremely unlikely. | Base, Arbitrum, HyperEVM |
| `instant` | API-confirmed events are final. No block/slot concept for ordering. | HyperCore |

The V2 Architecture RFC (P0-W1) originally used three finality labels. P0-W3
refined them to four by distinguishing `probabilistic-block` (Ethereum L1, real
reorg concern) from `deterministic-block` (L2 rollups, sequencer-final). The RFC
has been updated in `design/V2_ARCHITECTURE_RFC.md` to use the four-value set.

---

## 3. Six Required Worked Examples

Each example shows a `networks` row and a representative V2 checkpoint cursor.

### 3.1 Solana Mainnet

**Network row:** `solana-mainnet`, chain family `solana`, finality `probabilistic-slot`, block time 400ms.

**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
```json
{
  "target_id": "<uuid>",
  "network": "solana-mainnet",
  "source": "rpc",
  "cursor": {
    "last_signature": "5VERv8NMhzgC4...",
    "last_slot": 298412345,
    "commitment": "finalized"
  }
}
```

**gRPC checkpoint cursor:**
```json
{
  "target_id": "<uuid>",
  "network": "solana-mainnet",
  "source": "grpc",
  "cursor": {
    "last_slot": 298412400,
    "commitment": "confirmed"
  }
}
```

RPC and gRPC sources use different pagination primitives (signature vs slot) and
have independent checkpoint rows keyed by `(target_id, network, source)`.

### 3.2 Ethereum Mainnet

**Network row:** `ethereum-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `probabilistic-block`, block time 12000ms.

**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
```json
{
  "target_id": "<uuid>",
  "network": "ethereum-mainnet",
  "source": "rpc",
  "cursor": {
    "last_block": 21500000,
    "last_block_hash": "0x4e3a3754410177e6937ef1f84bba68ea139e8d1a..."
  }
}
```

Reorg detection uses `last_block_hash` comparison on checkpoint load.

### 3.3 Base Mainnet

**Network row:** `base-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `deterministic-block`, block time 2000ms.

**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
```json
{
  "target_id": "<uuid>",
  "network": "base-mainnet",
  "source": "rpc",
  "cursor": {
    "last_block": 25000000,
    "last_block_hash": "0xabc123..."
  }
}
```

Uses the same EVM connector as Ethereum. `deterministic-block` finality means
reorg detection is optional but `last_block_hash` is stored defensively.

### 3.4 Arbitrum Mainnet

**Network row:** `arbitrum-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `deterministic-block`, block time 250ms.

**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
```json
{
  "target_id": "<uuid>",
  "network": "arbitrum-mainnet",
  "source": "rpc",
  "cursor": {
    "last_block": 280000000,
    "last_block_hash": "0xdef456..."
  }
}
```

Fast block times (~250ms) may require larger `block_chunk` sizes for efficient
backfill. That is a connector configuration concern, not a network model concern.

### 3.5 HyperCore Mainnet

**Network row:** `hypercore-mainnet`, chain family `hyperliquid`, finality `instant`, block time NULL.

**REST checkpoint cursor:**
```json
{
  "target_id": "<uuid>",
  "network": "hypercore-mainnet",
  "source": "rest",
  "cursor": {
    "last_timestamp_ms": 1700000000001,
    "last_fill_tid": 987654,
    "data_types_covered": ["fills", "funding", "ledger_updates"]
  }
}
```

deduplication.

### 3.6 HyperEVM Mainnet

**Network row:** `hyperevm-mainnet`, chain family `evm`, finality `deterministic-block`, block time 2000ms.

**RPC checkpoint cursor:**
```json
{
  "target_id": "<uuid>",
  "network": "hyperevm-mainnet",
  "source": "rpc",
  "cursor": {
    "last_block": 5000000,
    "last_block_hash": "0x789abc..."
  }
}
```

HyperEVM is an EVM chain. It uses the standard EVM connector with a HyperEVM RPC
URL. See Section 4 for the routing split.

---

## 4. HyperCore vs HyperEVM Routing Split

HyperCore and HyperEVM are separate ingestion models despite being part of the
same Hyperliquid ecosystem.

| Property | HyperCore | HyperEVM |
|---|---|---|
| Chain family | `hyperliquid` | `evm` |
| Network ID | `hypercore-mainnet` | `hyperevm-mainnet` |
| Protocol model | Order book / clearinghouse | EVM smart contracts |
| Ingestion method | REST API + WebSocket | `eth_getLogs` + `eth_getBlockByNumber` |
| Finality | Instant (API-confirmed) | Deterministic block (sequencer-confirmed) |
| Checkpoint model | Timestamp + trade ID cursor | Block number + block hash cursor |

**Connector routing is determined by `chain_family`, not by ecosystem:**

```
Target on hypercore-mainnet → chain_family = hyperliquid → HyperliquidRestConnector / HyperliquidWsConnector
Target on hyperevm-mainnet  → chain_family = evm         → EvmConnector
```

A Hyperliquid user wanting complete coverage creates targets on both networks.
Cross-chain event correlation (e.g. bridging between HyperCore and HyperEVM) is
a downstream Silver/Gold layer concern, not a Bronze ingestion concern.

---

## 5. Checkpoint Cursor Shapes (Summary)

| Chain Family | Cursor Shape | Primary Resume Field | Reorg Detection |
|---|---|---|---|
| `solana` | `{ last_signature, last_slot, commitment }` | `last_signature` (RPC), `last_slot` (gRPC) | Not needed at confirmed+; slot-skip handling via gRPC `from_slot` |
| `evm` | `{ last_block, last_block_hash, last_log_index }` | `last_block` | `last_block_hash` comparison on checkpoint load |
| `hyperliquid` | `{ last_timestamp_ms, last_fill_tid, data_types_covered }` | `last_timestamp_ms` | Not needed (instant finality) |

---

## 6. Phase 1 Legacy Checkpoint Migration Guidance

This section provides concrete guidance for migrating existing
`indexer_checkpoints` rows to V2 `checkpoints` rows during the dual-write
transition (P1-W4). It corrects three issues identified in local review.

### 6.1 Current Legacy Schema

From `migrations/20260217010000_add_indexer_checkpoints.sql`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE indexer_checkpoints (
    chain chain_enum NOT NULL,             -- 'solana', 'hyperliquid', 'ethereum'
    wallet_address TEXT NOT NULL,
    last_signature TEXT,
    last_slot BIGINT,
    last_timestamp BIGINT,
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (chain, wallet_address)
);
```

From `migrations/20260218000000_add_last_block_to_checkpoints.sql`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE indexer_checkpoints ADD COLUMN last_block BIGINT;
```

### 6.2 Solana: Persisted Resume Cursor Semantics

**Important correction from earlier draft:** The Solana gRPC adapter
(`adapters/src/solana_grpc.rs`) uses an in-memory `SlotCheckpoint` (an
`AtomicU64` at lines 51-75) for `from_slot` reconnection. The adapter
itself does not call `repo.save_checkpoint()` with slot-based state.

However, the CLI ingest path (`cli/src/main.rs`, lines 147-155) calls
`SolanaGrpcAdapter::fetch_history()` and then passes the resulting
transactions through `build_checkpoint()` (`adapters/src/repo.rs`,
lines 42-78) and `save_transactions_and_checkpoint()` (lines 607-621).
This means **gRPC-derived Solana `indexer_checkpoints` rows CAN exist**
in the database. These rows have the same schema as RPC-derived rows:

- `last_signature`: set to the latest transaction hash (from
  `build_checkpoint`, line 73)
- `last_slot`: extracted from `raw_metadata["slot"]` (lines 54-59);
  present on BOTH RPC and gRPC-derived Solana transactions because both
  adapter outputs include `"slot"` in their `raw_metadata`
- `last_timestamp`: set to the latest transaction timestamp (line 76)

**The legacy `indexer_checkpoints` schema cannot distinguish RPC-derived
from gRPC-derived rows.** Both sources produce identical checkpoint
shapes through `build_checkpoint()`.

**Resume cursor semantics by adapter:**

| Adapter | Persisted field used for resume | How resume works |
|---|---|---|
| Solana RPC (`adapters/src/solana.rs`, lines 38-40) | `last_signature` | Passed as the `until` parameter to `getSignaturesForAddress`; the RPC returns transactions newer than this signature. |
| Solana gRPC via CLI (`cli/src/main.rs`, lines 149-152) | `last_slot` | CLI reads `checkpoint.last_slot`, calls `adapter.checkpoint().update(slot as u64)` to seed the in-memory `SlotCheckpoint`, then `fetch_history` uses `self.checkpoint.get()` as `from_slot`. |

**Why `last_signature` is the only authoritative persisted resume cursor:**

- `last_signature` is the **only** persisted cursor that an adapter reads
  directly for pagination. The Solana RPC adapter reads
  `checkpoint.last_signature` (line 38-40) and passes it to the RPC as
  the `until` parameter.
- `last_slot` is used by the CLI gRPC path indirectly (CLI code seeds the
  in-memory `SlotCheckpoint`), but it is **not** a V2 gRPC checkpoint
  equivalent: it carries no `commitment`-level metadata, may not reflect
  the gRPC adapter's actual in-memory slot state at process exit, and is
  present on RPC-derived rows too.
- Because RPC and gRPC-derived rows are indistinguishable in the legacy
  schema, the migration defaults all legacy Solana rows to
  `source = "rpc"` with `last_signature` as the primary cursor. This is
  safe for RPC resume.
- Legacy gRPC users will need to create fresh V2 gRPC checkpoints when
  Phase 2 gRPC connectors start persisting `(last_slot, commitment)` state
  directly to the `checkpoints` table.

**Migration mapping for Solana:**

| Old field | V2 cursor field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `last_signature` | `cursor.last_signature` | Authoritative RPC resume cursor; present on all legacy Solana rows regardless of original adapter |
| `last_slot` | `cursor.last_slot` | Informational only; present on all legacy Solana rows; not promoted to V2 gRPC cursor state |
| N/A | `source` | Default `"rpc"` for all legacy Solana rows; gRPC-derived rows cannot be reliably distinguished |
| N/A | `cursor.commitment` | Not tracked in legacy schema; omit or default to `"finalized"` (RPC `getSignaturesForAddress` returns finalized by default) |

### 6.3 HyperCore: Timestamp Precision Caveat

**Caveat (corrected from earlier draft):** The current Hyperliquid adapter
(`adapters/src/hyperliquid.rs`, lines 182-185) stores `last_timestamp` in
the `indexer_checkpoints` table as **seconds** (epoch seconds). The
conversion happens at line 200: `timestamp: (fill.time / 1000) as i64`,
which truncates milliseconds.

The V2 checkpoint cursor uses `last_timestamp_ms` (milliseconds). A naive
migration that multiplies by 1000 (`last_timestamp * 1000`) would produce
a value with **false millisecond precision**: the resulting timestamp would
always end in `000`, which is not the actual sub-second time of the last
event.

**Impact on resume semantics:**

- The current adapter resumes with `resume_ms = (checkpoint.last_timestamp * 1000) + 1` (line 184).
- After migration, if `last_timestamp_ms = last_timestamp * 1000`, the
  resume point becomes `last_timestamp_ms + 1`.
- This is equivalent to the current behavior and does **not** cause data
  loss.
- However, events that occurred in the same second as the checkpoint but
  after the truncated timestamp boundary will be **re-fetched** on resume.

**Required replay/dedupe semantics for Phase 1:**

1. The migration sets `cursor.last_timestamp_ms = last_timestamp * 1000`.
   The value is understood to have second-precision granularity rounded
   down to the millisecond boundary.
2. On first resume after migration, the connector must be prepared to see
   duplicate events from the final second of the previous run. The
   existing deduplication on `(network, tx_hash)` in `raw_transactions`
   handles this for transaction-level records.
3. For fills specifically, `last_fill_tid` is **not available** in legacy
   checkpoints. The migrated cursor omits `last_fill_tid`. The Phase 2
   HyperCore connector should use timestamp-only deduplication until a
   `last_fill_tid` is captured in the first post-migration checkpoint
   write.
4. New V2 checkpoint writes from the Phase 2 connector will store true
   millisecond timestamps directly from the API response (`fill.time`,
   `funding.time`, `update.time`), so the precision loss is a one-time
   migration artifact.

**Migration mapping for HyperCore:**

| Old field | V2 cursor field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `last_timestamp` | `cursor.last_timestamp_ms` | Multiply by 1000; understood as second-precision |
| N/A | `cursor.last_fill_tid` | Not available in legacy; omit |
| N/A | `source` | Always `"rest"` for legacy HyperCore rows |
| N/A | `cursor.data_types_covered` | Not tracked in legacy; omit or default to `["fills", "funding", "ledger_updates"]` |

### 6.4 EVM: Network Reclassification Caveat

**Caveat (carried from spec):** The current `Chain::Ethereum` variant
(`core/src/models.rs`, lines 6-10) is used for all EVM-compatible chains.
The repository maps it to the database string `"ethereum"`
(`adapters/src/repo.rs`, lines 4-9).

The migration defaults all legacy `chain = 'ethereum'` rows to
`network = 'ethereum-mainnet'`. This is correct for deployments that only
indexed Ethereum mainnet data via `Chain::Ethereum`.

**If a deployment was indexing Base, Arbitrum, or other EVM chain data
under `Chain::Ethereum`**, those rows will be incorrectly assigned to
`ethereum-mainnet`. This requires manual reclassification.

**Phase 1 must define the exact override mechanism before migration code
ships.** Options under consideration (to be resolved in P1-W2):

1. **Migration-time environment variable**: e.g.
   `REDACTED` forces all legacy
   Ethereum rows to a specific network. Simple but only works for
   single-network deployments.
2. **Migration-time configuration map**: a TOML or JSON map from
   `(chain, wallet_address)` to `network` for targeted reclassification.
3. **Post-migration reclassification CLI command**: a new CLI command to
   reassign `network` on existing rows by wallet address or block range.

The choice is deferred to P1-W2. This handoff documents the requirement
so it is not lost.

**Migration mapping for EVM:**

| Old field | V2 cursor field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `last_block` | `cursor.last_block` | Direct mapping |
| N/A | `cursor.last_block_hash` | Not tracked in legacy; omit (reorg detection starts fresh from V2) |
| N/A | `source` | Always `"rpc"` for legacy EVM rows |
| N/A | `network` | Default `"ethereum-mainnet"` unless overridden; see caveat above |

### 6.5 Legacy-to-V2 Default Source Summary

| Legacy `chain` value | V2 `chain_family` | V2 default `network` | V2 default `source` | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `solana` | `solana` | `solana-mainnet` | `rpc` | Legacy Solana checkpoints may come from either the RPC or gRPC CLI path but are indistinguishable in the legacy schema; `last_signature` is the authoritative persisted resume cursor (Section 6.2) |
| `hyperliquid` | `hyperliquid` | `hypercore-mainnet` | `rest` | All persisted HyperCore checkpoints come from the REST adapter |
| `ethereum` | `evm` | `ethereum-mainnet` | `rpc` | All persisted EVM checkpoints come from the RPC adapter; may need network reclassification (Section 6.4) |

---

## 7. Decisions Locked By This Handoff

These decisions are frozen. Phase 1+ work packets should reference them, not
reopen them.

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Three chain families | `solana`, `evm`, `hyperliquid` | Maps to three protocol-level ingestion models |
| HyperEVM is `evm`, not a fourth family | `hyperevm-mainnet` in chain family `evm` | HyperEVM uses standard EVM JSON-RPC |
| HyperCore is `hyperliquid` | `hypercore-mainnet` in chain family `hyperliquid` | HyperCore uses REST/WS, not EVM primitives |
| Network IDs are `{chain}-{env}` lowercase | e.g. `solana-mainnet`, `hypercore-mainnet` | Stable, readable, collision-free |
| Four finality models | `probabilistic-slot`, `probabilistic-block`, `deterministic-block`, `instant` | Distinguishes L1 reorg risk from L2 sequencer finality |
| Checkpoint cursor is JSONB | Per-family cursor shapes in Section 5 | Different chains need different cursor fields |
| `finality_model` is TEXT, not enum | Allows future refinement without migration | New chains may need new finality semantics |
| RPC URLs excluded from `networks` table | Deployment-specific config belongs in spectraplex.toml or env vars | Network registry stores protocol facts |
| HyperCore network ID is `hypercore-mainnet` | Not `hyperliquid-mainnet` | Avoids ambiguity with the broader ecosystem |
| `block_time_ms` is nullable | HyperCore has no block concept | Prevents meaningless zero values |

---

## 8. Terminology Cross-Reference

This section confirms alignment with the other Phase 0 specs.

### 8.1 V2 Architecture RFC (P0-W1) Alignment

**Taxonomy and finality alignment (verified):**

- `chain_family_enum` values: `solana, evm, hyperliquid` — **matches**
- Network ID examples: `solana-mainnet`, `ethereum-mainnet`, `base-mainnet` — **matches**
- Finality model labels: four-value set adopted from P0-W3 — **matches** (RFC Section 3.3 updated)
- HyperEVM routing: EVM connector with HyperEVM network — **matches**
- `networks` table schema: `rpc_url` removed, `block_time_ms` added — **matches** (RFC Section 3.3 updated)

**Checkpoint cursor shapes (partial alignment — P0-W3 extends the RFC):**

- The RFC Section 3.4 documents baseline cursor shapes: Solana
  `{ last_signature, last_slot }`, EVM `{ last_block, last_block_hash }`,
  Hyperliquid `{ last_timestamp, last_fill_tid }`.
- P0-W3 extends these with additional fields: `commitment` (Solana),
  `last_log_index` (EVM), `data_types_covered` (Hyperliquid).
- P0-W3 renames the Hyperliquid field `last_timestamp` to
  `last_timestamp_ms` to reflect that the V2 cursor stores millisecond
  precision directly (Section 6.3 documents the legacy second-precision
  caveat).
- The RFC's Section 3.4 inline JSONB comment (`{ last_signature,
  last_slot, last_block, last_timestamp, ... }`) and the Hyperliquid
  cursor field names have **not been updated** to reflect the P0-W3
  refinements. This is a documentation gap in `design/V2_ARCHITECTURE_RFC.md`,
  not a semantic conflict.
- **The authoritative cursor field definitions for Phase 1 are in this
  handoff (Section 5), not in the RFC.**

### 8.2 Target Model Spec (P0-W2) Alignment

- `index_targets.network` examples: `solana-mainnet`, `ethereum-mainnet`, `base-mainnet` — **matches**
- `index_targets.chain_family` values: `solana, evm, hyperliquid` — **matches**
- HyperEVM contract target routing: EVM chain family with `hyperevm-mainnet` — **matches**
- HyperCore target examples use `hypercore-mainnet` — **matches** (corrected from `hyperliquid-mainnet` in P0-W3)

---

| EVM legacy network reclassification override mechanism | P1-W2 |

   115→| `transactions` are unique on `(chain, tx_hash)` while still carrying one wallet and one user | The same raw transaction cannot safely belong to multiple tracked wallets, users, or targets | Split raw transaction identity from target membership with join tables |
   116→| `LedgerEntry` is the main Silver abstraction | Great for tax, not enough for TVL, swaps, positions, funding, protocol state, or general ETL | Make ledger one materialization among several normalized datasets |
   117→| `Chain::Ethereum` is a single enum variant | "Ethereum" is a chain family, not a network. Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, HyperEVM, etc. should not be flattened away | Model `chain_family` and `network` separately |
   118→| CLI/API ingestion takes wallets, not generic filters | Limits Spectraplex to personal-wallet style indexing | Add ingest specs that support addresses, program IDs, contracts, topics, coins, and custom filters |
   119→| Query APIs are wallet scoped | Good app API, weak platform API | Add dataset-based and filter-based query/export interfaces |
   120→| Metadata resolution is hardcoded | Static token symbol/decimal maps will not scale across chains and protocols | Add asset metadata services and caches |
   121→
   122→### Code-level concerns that matter strategically
   123→
   124→These are not small cosmetic issues. They point directly at where the current architecture will block your broader goal.
   125→
   126→1. **The raw model is too consumer-shaped.**
   127→
   128→   In `core/src/models.rs`, `Transaction` includes `user_id` and `wallet_address`. That makes the Bronze layer less reusable than it should be. Raw chain data should be canonical and target-agnostic.
   129→
   130→2. **The storage model cannot represent one raw transaction linked to multiple tracked subjects.**
   131→
   132→   In `migrations/20260217100000_add_unique_chain_tx_hash.sql`, raw transactions are unique on `(chain, tx_hash)`, but the row also stores a single `wallet_address` and `user_id`. That is a structural mismatch.
   133→
   134→   Example: if two tracked wallets appear in the same transaction, or two users track the same wallet, the raw record model becomes ambiguous.
   135→
   136→3. **The repo and API are centered on `wallet_address`.**
   137→
   138→   `adapters/src/repo.rs`, `cli/src/main.rs`, and `api/src/main.rs` are built around wallet-based ingestion, normalization, and queries. That is useful, but it is not a general indexing substrate yet.
   139→
   140→4. **The current EVM adapter is not aligned with wallet-history indexing, and it is also not yet a generic contract indexer.**
   141→
   142→   In `adapters/src/evm.rs`, `eth_getLogs` is called with the supplied wallet as the `address` filter. For normal wallets, that means "logs emitted by this address," not "logs involving this wallet." That is not correct for wallet transfer indexing, and it is also not a general contract/topic indexing API yet.
   143→
   144→5. **The current Solana gRPC path does not match the wallet abstraction it is exposed through.**
   145→
   146→   In `adapters/src/solana_grpc.rs`, the subscription filter is built from program IDs, not from the requested wallet. `fetch_history()` then stamps the caller's wallet onto whatever matching transactions arrive. That is a sign that the abstraction is wrong, not just incomplete.
   147→
   148→6. **The real-time Solana stream path currently produces raw transactions without a meaningful tracked subject.**
   149→
   150→   The stream endpoint persists transactions from the gRPC stream, but those streamed records are not tied to a wallet or more general target model in a principled way.
   151→
   152→7. **The Silver layer is still heavily tax-ledger shaped.**
   153→
   154→   `LedgerEntry` is good, but for your broader goal you also need normalized primitives like:
   155→
   156→   - token transfers
   157→   - native balance deltas
   158→   - decoded contract events
   159→   - Solana instruction records
   160→   - DEX swaps
   161→   - perpetual fills
   162→   - funding payments
   163→   - protocol position snapshots
   164→   - pool state snapshots
   165→
   166→8. **The current API looks like an app API, not an indexing platform API.**
   167→
   168→   It is useful, but it is optimized for wallet retrieval rather than generic dataset delivery or ETL-friendly exports.
   169→
   170→## 6. The Use Cases You Care About, Mapped Honestly
   171→
   172→| Use case | Fit today | Why | What unlocks it |
   173→| --- | --- | --- | --- |
   174→| Crypto tax calculator | Medium | Bronze/Silver ledger path exists | canonical raw storage, multi-wallet linking, price service, tax-lot logic |
   175→| Hyperliquid-only dashboard | Medium | Hyperliquid adapter and parser exist | market/user filter model, stronger WS persistence, positions and funding datasets |
   176→| Cross-chain wallet dashboard | Medium | wallet-oriented APIs already exist | better network model, stronger asset metadata, price service, completeness tracking |
   177→| DeFi TVL dashboard | Low | no pool/protocol/state target model | contract/program/pool targets, protocol datasets, snapshot materializers |
   178→| Generic ETL layer | Low | no sink abstraction, no generic dataset API | dataset registry, export/sink pipeline, canonical raw model |
   179→| Protocol-specific multi-chain indexer | Low to Medium | adapters exist, abstractions do not | filter-driven ingestion specs and target registry |
   180→
   181→The conclusion is straightforward:
   182→
   183→**You already have a strong wallet-indexing foundation.**
   184→
   185→**You do not yet have a general-purpose indexing substrate.**
   186→
   187→That is fixable, but it requires changing the shape of the core model, not just adding more endpoints.
   188→
   189→## 7. Recommended Product Direction
   190→
   191→The best path is:
   192→
   193→**Build Spectraplex as a general indexing core with wallet/tax as the first high-value materialization.**
   194→
   195→That means:
   196→
   197→- keep the wallet use case because it is concrete and useful
   198→- keep wallet indexing first-class as a target model and downstream materialization
   199→- stop treating the wallet view as the only first-class view
   200→- elevate "target registration", "dataset normalization", and "ETL export" to core product concepts
   201→
   202→This is the right compromise between the earlier docs' "portfolio/tax" framing and your stated "multi-purpose indexing layer" goal.
   203→
   204→## 8. Target Architecture
   205→
   206→### 8.1 Core principle
   207→
   208→Ingest raw chain data once. Normalize it into reusable datasets. Materialize specialized views later.
   209→
   210→### 8.2 Recommended layers
   211→
   212→```text
   213→Connectors -> Bronze raw data -> Silver normalized datasets -> Gold/materialized views -> ETL sinks / APIs
   214→```
   215→
   216→### 8.3 Bronze layer
   217→
   218→The Bronze layer should contain canonical raw chain facts, not user-shaped rows.
   219→
   220→Recommended Bronze datasets:
   221→
   222→- raw blocks / slots
   223→- raw transactions
   224→- raw Solana instruction payloads
   225→- raw EVM logs
   226→- raw Hyperliquid API payloads
   227→- raw ingestion metadata (source, cursor, checkpoint, run id, observed_at, finalized_at)
   228→
   229→### 8.4 Silver layer
   230→
   231→The Silver layer should no longer be only `ledger_entries`.
   232→
   233→Recommended reusable Silver datasets:
   234→
   235→- token transfers
   236→- native balance deltas
   237→- contract events
   238→- Solana instruction records
   239→- decoded swaps
   240→- Hyperliquid fills
   241→- Hyperliquid funding payments
   242→- position changes
   243→- balance snapshots
   244→
   245→### 8.5 Gold/materialized views
   246→
   247→These should be derived, not foundational:
   248→
   249→- wallet ledger
   250→- balance history
   251→- tax-lot views
   252→- PnL views
   253→- TVL snapshots
   254→- protocol dashboards
   255→- warehouse-ready exports
   256→
   257→### 8.6 Control-plane concepts the repo needs
   258→
   259→Add first-class concepts for:
   260→
   261→- `network`
   262→- `connector`
   263→- `index_target`
   264→- `ingestion_run`
   265→- `checkpoint`
   266→- `completeness_window`
   267→- `dataset_version`
   268→- `materialization_job`
   269→- `sink`
   270→
   271→### 8.7 Better abstraction for indexing targets
   272→
   273→Spectraplex needs a target model like:
   274→
   275→```text
   276→IndexTarget
   277→- id
   278→- kind: wallet | contract | program | topic_filter | market | pool | protocol
   279→- chain_family
   280→- network
   281→- filter_spec (JSONB or typed structs)
   282→- mode: backfill | stream | both
   283→```
   284→
   285→That one change would make the system far more general.
   286→
   287→### 8.8 Better chain and network model
   288→
   289→Do not flatten everything into `solana`, `hyperliquid`, and `ethereum`.
   290→
   291→A better model is:
   292→
   293→- `chain_family`: solana | evm | hyperliquid
   294→- `network`: solana-mainnet | ethereum-mainnet | base-mainnet | arbitrum-mainnet | hyperevm-mainnet | etc.
   295→
   296→This matters for:
   297→
   298→- RPC routing
   299→- chain-specific finality logic
   300→- token metadata
   301→- checkpoint semantics
   302→- downstream analytics
   303→
   304→### 8.9 Connector model
   305→
   306→The current `ChainIngestor` trait is too narrow as the main long-term abstraction.
   307→
   308→It should evolve toward something filter-driven, not wallet-driven.
   309→
   310→At minimum, Spectraplex needs connectors that can support:
   311→
   312→- historical backfill
   313→- real-time streaming
   314→- checkpoint resume
   315→- gap fill
   316→- finality or reorg semantics
   317→
   318→### 8.10 Delivery model
   319→
   320→If Spectraplex is meant to plug into ETL flows, delivery cannot stop at "query this REST endpoint."
   321→
   322→It should support:
   323→
   324→- REST query APIs
   325→- JSONL export
   326→- CSV export where useful
   327→- Parquet export
   328→- webhooks
   329→- database-to-database materialization
   330→- object storage sinks
   331→- later, queue sinks if they become justified
   332→
   333→## 9. Chain-Specific Guidance To Keep
   334→
   335→These are the most useful chain-specific conclusions from the research docs and conceptual notes.
   336→
   337→### Solana
   338→
   339→- Use transaction-based indexing for ledger and financial use cases.
   340→- Use Yellowstone gRPC for real-time where possible.
   341→- Use RPC or an accelerated provider for backfills.
   342→- Treat confirmed vs finalized carefully.
   343→- Expect instruction parsing, CPI handling, and token metadata resolution to matter.
   344→
   345→### Hyperliquid
   346→
   347→- Treat HyperCore and HyperEVM as two different ingestion modes.
   348→- HyperCore is API/WebSocket-native, not block-scan-native.
   349→- Hyperliquid is a strong differentiator because many generic indexers do not cover its trading layer well.
   350→- Funding, fills, and position changes should be first-class datasets.
   351→
   352→### EVM
   353→
   354→- Use `eth_getLogs` and later `eth_subscribe` as core primitives.
   355→- Model reorgs explicitly.
   356→- Separate "wallet activity indexing" from "contract event indexing" because they are different problems.
   357→- ABI decoding should feed reusable Silver datasets, not just ledger entries.
   358→
   359→## 10. Phased Plan To Move The Project Forward
   360→
   361→## Phase 0: Reframe The Project
   362→
   363→**Goal:** Shift the repo from wallet app shape to indexing-platform shape.
   364→
   365→Deliverables:
   366→
   367→- write and commit the v2 architecture RFC
   368→- define target kinds and network model
   369→- define Bronze/Silver/Gold boundaries
   370→- decide what Spectraplex owns vs what downstream ETL owns
   371→
   372→Exit criteria:
   373→
   374→- team agrees that ledger is one output, not the output
   375→- network model is approved
   376→- target model is approved
   377→
   378→## Phase 1: Fix The Core Data Model
   379→
   380→**Goal:** Make raw chain data canonical and reusable.
   381→
   382→Deliverables:
   383→
   384→- create canonical raw transaction tables independent of wallet/user
   385→- add `index_targets`
   386→- add link tables from raw data to targets
   387→- add `ingestion_runs`, `checkpoints`, and `completeness_windows`
   388→- separate `chain_family` from `network`
   389→
   390→Recommended schema direction:
   391→
   392→- `raw_transactions`
   393→- `raw_blocks`
   394→- `raw_evm_logs`
   395→- `raw_solana_instructions`
   396→- `raw_hyperliquid_events`
   397→- `index_targets`
   398→- `target_matches`
   399→- `ingestion_runs`
   400→- `dataset_versions`
   401→
   402→Exit criteria:
   403→
   404→- the same raw transaction can be linked to multiple targets safely
   405→- raw data no longer depends on `wallet_address` for identity
   406→
   407→## Phase 2: Correct The Ingestion Abstractions
   408→
   409→**Goal:** Replace wallet-only ingestion with filter-based ingestion.
   410→
   411→Deliverables:
   412→
   413→- evolve `ChainIngestor` into a filter-driven connector model
   414→- add target specs for wallets, contracts, programs, topics, and Hyperliquid users/markets
   415→- fix the EVM connector semantics
   416→- fix the Solana gRPC connector semantics
   417→- support both backfill and stream modes per target
   418→
   419→Exit criteria:
   420→
   421→- a target can be registered without pretending it is a wallet
   422→- EVM wallet activity and contract event indexing are both supported via explicit modes
   423→- Solana gRPC filters map to actual requested targets
   424→
   425→## Phase 3: Expand The Silver Layer
   426→
   427→**Goal:** Turn Spectraplex into a reusable normalization engine.
   428→
   429→Deliverables:
   430→
   431→- keep `ledger_entries` but demote it to one dataset among several
   432→- add normalized transfer datasets
   433→- add decoded event datasets
   434→- add swap/fill/funding datasets
   435→- add position and balance snapshot datasets
   436→- introduce parser/materializer versioning
   437→
   438→Exit criteria:
   439→
   440→- a downstream system can consume a protocol/event dataset without going through wallet-ledger semantics
   441→
   442→## Phase 4: Build ETL-First Delivery
   443→
   444→**Goal:** Make Spectraplex easy to plug into external systems.
   445→
   446→Deliverables:
   447→
   448→- generic export jobs
   449→- dataset-based API endpoints
   450→- JSONL and Parquet outputs
   451→- webhook and database sink options
   452→- run metadata and completeness metadata in all exports
   453→
   454→Exit criteria:
   455→
   456→- Spectraplex can act as a source of truth for another ETL or BI pipeline
   457→
   458→## Phase 5: Ship Reference Use-Case Packs
   459→
   460→**Goal:** Prove the platform through downstream materializations.
   461→
   462→Recommended first packs:
   463→
   464→- wallet ledger / balances / tax export pack
   465→- Hyperliquid trader analytics pack
   466→- protocol event and TVL pack
   467→
   468→Exit criteria:
   469→
   470→- at least two very different downstream products are powered by the same indexing core
   471→
   472→## 11. Immediate Backlog I Would Start With
   473→
   474→If I were continuing this repo today, I would do these in this order:
   475→
   476→1. Write a v2 schema and connector RFC based on the architecture above.
   477→2. Remove consumer identity from the Bronze model.
   478→3. Introduce `network` and `index_target` tables.
   479→4. Replace wallet-only ingest requests with a generic ingest spec while keeping wallet compatibility temporarily.
   480→5. Fix the EVM ingestion path so wallet activity and contract event indexing are explicit, correct modes.
   481→6. Fix the Solana gRPC path so subscriptions are tied to real target filters instead of stamped wallet labels.
   482→7. Create Silver datasets for token transfers and decoded protocol events, not only ledger entries.
   483→8. Add completeness/run metadata everywhere.
   484→9. Add export sinks for JSONL and Parquet.
   485→10. Build one reference downstream consumer for wallets and one for protocol analytics.
   486→
   487→## 12. What Not To Do
   488→
   489→These earlier docs were right about several anti-patterns. I agree with them.
   490→
   491→- Do not add Kafka, NATS, or Redis Streams yet unless you have a real throughput or multi-worker need.
   492→- Do not build a full frontend before the indexing model is correct.
   493→- Do not try to index every chain or every protocol at once.
   494→- Do not turn PostgreSQL into the problem before it actually becomes the problem.
   495→- Do not keep growing a wallet-only abstraction if the product goal is broader.
   496→
   497→## 13. Final Assessment
   498→
   499→Spectraplex already has a strong foundation:
   500→
   501→- good language choice
   502→- good repo structure
   503→- correct instinct around Bronze/Silver layering
   504→- meaningful chain coverage
   505→- real code, not just design notes
   506→
   507→But if the real goal is an all-purpose multi-chain indexing layer for many ETL consumers, the project now needs a **structural refactor of its core abstractions**.
   508→
   509→The most important change is this:
   510→
   511→**move from a wallet-centric transaction indexer to a target-centric data platform**
   512→
   513→If you make that shift, the tax calculator, Hyperliquid dashboard, and TVL dashboard all become natural downstream products of the same core system.
   514→
   515→If you do not make that shift, Spectraplex will stay useful, but it will mostly remain a wallet-history ingester with some extra adapters.
   516→
